tool.name: LlamaIndex
tool.tagline: Data framework for LLM apps: RAG over your documents, agents and workflows
tool.description: LlamaIndex is a Python framework for connecting LLMs to your own data. It loads documents, splits and embeds them into indexes, and answers questions through query engines, chat engines and retrievers; on top of that it offers tool-using agents and event-driven Workflows. It integrates with hundreds of model providers and vector databases, and with LlamaParse for document parsing.

glossary.def: In LlamaIndex, your chunks (nodes) stored and organised so the ones most relevant to a question can be found quickly, like the index at the back of a book.
A multi-step AI program whose steps are planned in advance. In LlamaIndex, a Workflow is a class whose steps react to events; even its agents are built as Workflows.
LlamaIndex's object for one whole source, such as a file or a web page: its text plus metadata.
In LlamaIndex, one chunk of a Document with its own text, metadata and id. Nodes are what get embedded, retrieved and shown to the LLM.
In LlamaIndex, code that loads a source (a folder, Notion, a database...) and returns a list of Document objects.
LlamaIndex's catalogue of integrations: hundreds of readers, model connectors, vector stores and tools, each installed as its own package.
In LlamaIndex, the component that cuts Documents into nodes (chunks), for example SentenceSplitter.
In LlamaIndex, any step applied to documents or nodes during ingestion, such as a node parser, a metadata extractor or the embedding model.
LlamaIndex's most common index: it stores an embedding for every node and finds the nodes closest in meaning to a question.
In LlamaIndex, the storage that keeps node texts and metadata (and document ids), next to the vectors.
In LlamaIndex, the small store of bookkeeping about an index: which nodes belong to it and how it is set up.
LlamaIndex's container that groups the stores an index uses: vector store, docstore and index store.
A LlamaIndex object that takes a question and returns an answer: a retriever finds relevant nodes, then a response synthesizer has the LLM write the answer.
A LlamaIndex object that does only the search half: question in, a ranked list of nodes with scores out.
The LlamaIndex part that turns a question plus retrieved nodes into an answer by prompting the LLM.
The strategy a LlamaIndex response synthesizer uses to fit retrieved text into prompts, such as compact, refine or tree_summarize.
A LlamaIndex object for conversations over your data: it keeps the chat history so follow-up questions make sense.
In LlamaIndex, a step between retrieval and the LLM that drops, reorders or changes the retrieved nodes.
In LlamaIndex, the storage that holds the embeddings and runs similarity search: the built-in in-memory one, or a vector database through an integration.
A condition on node metadata (such as year >= 2024 or department = hr) that restricts which nodes a search may return.
Getting data into a RAG system: loading it, splitting it into chunks, embedding them and storing the result.
LlamaIndex's reusable chain of transformations for ingestion; it can skip unchanged documents and write straight to a vector store.
A LlamaIndex transformation that asks an LLM to add metadata to each node, such as a title, summary or questions it answers.
A popular Python library for describing the shape of data with classes and type hints, and checking that real data matches it.
A free app that downloads open-weight models and runs them on your own computer, so nothing is sent to an online provider.
LlamaIndex's paid online service for turning hard documents (PDFs with tables, scans, slides) into clean Markdown or JSON.
The older name of LlamaIndex's hosted platform (now presented as LlamaParse), and the name of its current Python SDK package, llama-cloud.
LlamaIndex's standard agent: an LLM that calls tools through the model's built-in tool calling, in a loop, until it can answer.
A LlamaIndex wrapper that turns a whole query engine into one tool an agent can call, described by a name and a description.
In a multi-agent setup, one agent passing control of the conversation to another, more suitable agent.
LlamaIndex's built-in way to run several agents that pass control to each other (handoffs) and share state.
A second, more careful model that re-scores the passages a search returned and keeps only the best few.
A model that reads a question and a passage together and outputs how relevant the passage is; more accurate, but slower, than comparing two embeddings.
A classic keyword-search scoring method that ranks passages by how often the question's exact words appear in them, adjusted for length and rarity.
Searching with both meaning (vector search) and exact words (keyword search such as BM25), then merging the two result lists.
A simple way to merge several ranked lists: each item scores more the higher it appears in any list, so items near the top of either list rise.
Mean reciprocal rank: a retrieval score that rewards finding the right item near the top (1 if first, 0.5 if second, 0.33 if third...), averaged over questions.
Whether an answer is backed by the retrieved text rather than made up; LlamaIndex's FaithfulnessEvaluator checks it with an LLM.
Hypothetical document embeddings: have the LLM write a guessed answer, then search with that answer's embedding instead of the question's.
In tracing, one timed piece of work (such as a retrieval or an LLM call), nested inside bigger ones to form a tree for each request.
Code built into a program that reports what it is doing (events, timings, inputs and outputs) so you can trace and measure it.

concepts.name: What LlamaIndex is
concepts.summary: Understand what LlamaIndex does, its RAG pipeline, and how the core and integration packages fit together.
concepts.why: Knowing the pipeline and the package layout prevents import errors and confusion from outdated tutorials.
concepts.body:
Imagine asking a question about your company's 500-page handbook and getting an answer with the exact paragraphs it came from. That is what **LlamaIndex** is built for: connecting LLMs to *your* data.

Its core job is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), done in stages:

- **Load**: read files, web pages or databases into `Document` objects, one per source.
- **Index**: split documents into small chunks called **nodes**, turn them into embeddings and store them. The stored, searchable result is the **index**, like the index at the back of a book.
- **Query**: when someone asks a question (a **query**), find the most relevant chunks and give them to the LLM to write an answer.

On top of that, LlamaIndex has **agents** (LLMs that use tools, including your indexes, in a loop) and **Workflows**: multi-step AI programs whose steps you plan in advance. Each step runs when the step before it sends a message, called an event.

**Packages.** LlamaIndex is split into many pip packages:

- `llama-index-core`: all the core classes. Imports start with `llama_index.core`.
- **Integrations** (connectors to outside services such as model providers and databases), one package each: `llama-index-llms-openai`, `llama-index-llms-anthropic`, `llama-index-llms-ollama`, `llama-index-embeddings-huggingface`, `llama-index-vector-stores-chroma` and hundreds more. Their imports look like `llama_index.llms.openai`.
- `llama-index`: a starter bundle with core plus the OpenAI integrations.

Older tutorials (before version 0.10) import from `llama_index` directly, use `ServiceContext`, or build agents with `OpenAIAgent` and `ReActAgent.from_tools`. Those APIs are gone or outdated. Current code uses `Settings`, `llama_index.core` imports and workflow-based agents such as `FunctionAgent`.
concepts.code:
# pip install llama-index            # core + OpenAI LLM and embeddings
# pip install llama-index-llms-ollama llama-index-vector-stores-chroma   # extras as needed
import importlib.metadata as md

for pkg in ["llama-index-core", "llama-index-llms-openai", "llama-index-embeddings-openai"]:
    try:
        print(f"{pkg:32} {md.version(pkg)}")
    except md.PackageNotFoundError:
        print(f"{pkg:32} not installed")
# llama-index-core                 0.14.x

from llama_index.core import VectorStoreIndex, Settings     # core classes
from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI                   # an integration package
takeaways: Pipeline: load, index (chunk + embed + store), query
`llama-index-core` plus one package per integration
Pre-0.10 imports, ServiceContext and OpenAIAgent are outdated
pitfalls: Following a 2023 tutorial that uses ServiceContext or `from llama_index import ...`, which fails on current versions.

quiz.q: You want to use a Chroma vector database with LlamaIndex. What do you install?
options: Nothing; every integration is in llama-index-core
quiz.explain: Each integration lives in its own package; vector stores use the llama-index-vector-stores-* naming.

concepts.name: Your first RAG app in five lines
concepts.summary: Load a folder, build a VectorStoreIndex, and ask questions with a query engine.
concepts.why: Seeing the whole pipeline work end to end first makes every later component easier to place.
concepts.body:
The smallest useful LlamaIndex program answers questions about a folder of files:

```python
documents = SimpleDirectoryReader("data").load_data()
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(documents)
query_engine = index.as_query_engine()
response = query_engine.query("What is our refund policy?")
print(response)
```

What happens behind these lines:

1. `SimpleDirectoryReader` reads every supported file in `data/` (text, PDF, Word, Markdown and more) into `Document` objects. Markdown is text with simple formatting marks, like `#` for a heading.
2. `VectorStoreIndex.from_documents` splits the documents into chunks, sends each chunk to an embedding model and keeps the resulting **vectors** (the lists of numbers that capture meaning) in memory, so they vanish when the program ends.
3. `as_query_engine()` builds a **query engine**, an object that, for each question, embeds the question, finds the most similar chunks (2 by default), puts them into a prompt, and asks the LLM to answer from them.
4. `query` returns a `Response`. Printing it shows the answer; `response.source_nodes` lists the chunks that were used, with similarity scores.

By default LlamaIndex uses OpenAI for both the LLM and the embeddings, so first set the `OPENAI_API_KEY` **environment variable**: a named setting your program can read when it starts, often used for API keys. The next lesson shows how to choose other models, including local ones.

Always look at `source_nodes` when an answer seems wrong. If the right chunk isn't there, the problem is retrieval, not the LLM, and no prompt change will fix it.
concepts.code:
# pip install llama-index ; export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
from llama_index.core import SimpleDirectoryReader, VectorStoreIndex

documents = SimpleDirectoryReader("data").load_data()   # every file in ./data
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(documents)     # chunk + embed + store
query_engine = index.as_query_engine()

response = query_engine.query("How long do refunds take?")
print(response)                    # Refunds are processed within 5 business days.

for src in response.source_nodes:  # the chunks the answer was based on
    print(round(src.score, 2), src.node.metadata["file_name"])
# 0.83 refunds.md
# 0.71 faq.md
takeaways: Load with `SimpleDirectoryReader`, then `VectorStoreIndex.from_documents`, then `as_query_engine().query()`
The default LLM and embeddings are OpenAI's (needs OPENAI_API_KEY)
`response.source_nodes` shows which chunks the answer used
pitfalls: Judging a RAG app only by its answers without checking source_nodes, so retrieval problems look like model problems.

quiz.q: A query answer is wrong and source_nodes shows unrelated chunks. Where is the problem most likely?
options: Retrieval: chunking, embeddings or the number of chunks retrieved
quiz.explain: If the right chunks were never retrieved, the LLM had no way to answer correctly.

concepts.name: Settings: LLMs and embedding models
concepts.summary: Choose the LLM and embedding model globally with Settings or per component, including local models via Ollama.
concepts.why: Model choice sets quality, cost, privacy and speed, and mixing up embedding models silently breaks retrieval.
concepts.body:
LlamaIndex uses two kinds of models:

- an **LLM**, which writes answers, and
- an **embedding model**, which turns text into vectors for search.

**`Settings`** is a global object holding the defaults every component uses:

```python
Settings.llm = OpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0)
Settings.embed_model = OpenAIEmbedding(model="text-embedding-3-small")
```

Set these once at program start. You can also pass `llm=` or `embed_model=` to a single component (for example `index.as_query_engine(llm=other_llm)`) to override the default there.

Each provider is its own package: `llama-index-llms-anthropic` gives `Anthropic`, `llama-index-llms-ollama` gives `Ollama`, `llama-index-embeddings-huggingface` gives `HuggingFaceEmbedding`, and so on. Model names change often, so check the provider's current list.

**Local models.** With **Ollama** (a free app that runs open-weight models on your own machine), use `Ollama(model="llama3.1", request_timeout=120.0)` for the LLM and `OllamaEmbedding` or `HuggingFaceEmbedding(model_name="BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5")` for embeddings. Nothing leaves your computer, but local LLMs are slower and less capable.

`Settings` also holds defaults such as `chunk_size` (1024 tokens) and `chunk_overlap`.

The most important rule: **index and query with the same embedding model.** Vectors from different models are not comparable. If you change the embedding model, rebuild the index.
concepts.code:
# pip install llama-index-llms-ollama llama-index-embeddings-huggingface
from llama_index.core import Settings
from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI
from llama_index.embeddings.openai import OpenAIEmbedding

Settings.llm = OpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0)                 # OPENAI_API_KEY
Settings.embed_model = OpenAIEmbedding(model="text-embedding-3-small")
Settings.chunk_size = 512                                                  # default 1024

# Fully local alternative (Ollama running on this machine):
# from llama_index.llms.ollama import Ollama
# from llama_index.embeddings.huggingface import HuggingFaceEmbedding
# Settings.llm = Ollama(model="llama3.1", request_timeout=120.0)
# Settings.embed_model = HuggingFaceEmbedding(model_name="BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5")

vec = Settings.embed_model.get_text_embedding("hello world")
print(len(vec))                          # 1536 for text-embedding-3-small
print(Settings.llm.complete("Say hi in 3 words.").text)
takeaways: `Settings.llm` and `Settings.embed_model` set global defaults
Override per component with `llm=` or `embed_model=`
Index and query with the same embedding model; re-index after changing it
pitfalls: Switching Settings.embed_model while loading an index built with another model, which returns nonsense matches without any error.

quiz.q: You change the embedding model and load an index saved yesterday. What should you do?
options: Rebuild the index with the new embedding model
quiz.explain: Vectors from different embedding models live in different spaces, so the index must be rebuilt.

concepts.name: Loading data with readers
concepts.summary: Load files with SimpleDirectoryReader options and other sources with LlamaHub readers.
concepts.why: What you load and how determines everything downstream; garbage in means garbage answers.
concepts.body:
A **reader** (also called a data connector) turns a source, such as a folder, a website or an app, into a list of `Document` objects. A **Document** holds one source's text plus details about it.

**`SimpleDirectoryReader`** handles local files and is built in. It picks how to read each file from the end of its name (`.txt`, `.md`, `.pdf`...): text files and Markdown, PDF, Word, PowerPoint, CSV, images and more (some types need extra packages such as `pypdf`). Useful options:

- `input_dir="data"` or `input_files=["a.pdf", "b.md"]`.
- `recursive=True` to include subfolders.
- `required_exts=[".md", ".pdf"]` to load only those types.
- `exclude=["*.tmp"]` to skip files.
- `filename_as_id=True` gives each document a stable id based on its path, which matters for updating an index later.
- `num_workers=4` loads four files at a time.

Each document gets **metadata** automatically: `file_name`, `file_path`, `file_type`, size and dates. Metadata travels with every chunk and is used for citations and filters.

For other sources, **LlamaHub** (LlamaIndex's catalogue of add-on packages) offers hundreds of readers, each a separate package: web pages, Notion, Google Drive, Slack, databases and more. They all return `Document` lists, so the rest of your code stays the same.

Complex PDFs with tables, two-column layouts or scanned pages often come out messy with simple readers. LlamaParse (a later lesson) is LlamaIndex's online service for those.

For huge folders, use `reader.iter_data()` to handle one file at a time instead of loading everything into memory.
concepts.code:
from llama_index.core import SimpleDirectoryReader

reader = SimpleDirectoryReader(
    input_dir="data",
    recursive=True,                    # include subfolders
    required_exts=[".md", ".txt", ".pdf"],
    filename_as_id=True,               # stable ids from file paths
)
docs = reader.load_data()
print(len(docs))                       # e.g. 12
print(docs[0].metadata["file_name"])   # refunds.md
print(docs[0].doc_id)                  # .../data/refunds.md
print(docs[0].text[:40])               # Refunds are processed within 5 busin

for file_docs in reader.iter_data():   # one file at a time for big folders
    pass
takeaways: `SimpleDirectoryReader` loads many file types and adds file metadata
Use `recursive`, `required_exts` and `filename_as_id`
LlamaHub readers load other sources into the same Document type
pitfalls: Loading a whole folder including old copies and temporary files, which fills the index with duplicates and junk.

quiz.q: Why set filename_as_id=True when loading?
options: Each document gets a stable id from its path, so re-loading can update rather than duplicate
quiz.explain: Stable document ids let LlamaIndex recognise the same file later for updates and de-duplication.

concepts.name: Documents, nodes and metadata
concepts.summary: Work with Document and TextNode objects, attach metadata, and control what metadata the LLM and embeddings see.
concepts.why: Nodes and their metadata are the unit of retrieval, citation and filtering in every LlamaIndex app.
concepts.body:
A **Document** is a whole source, such as one file or one web page. A **node** (usually a `TextNode`) is a chunk of a document: the actual unit that gets embedded, retrieved and shown to the LLM.

Both carry:

- `text`: the content.
- `metadata`: a dictionary such as `{"file_name": "policy.pdf", "department": "hr", "year": 2025}`.
- an id: `doc_id` for documents, `node_id` for nodes.

When a document is split, each node copies the document's metadata and records a **relationship** back to its source (`node.ref_doc_id`), plus links to the previous and next nodes.

You can create documents yourself from any data, for example entries from a database: `Document(text=..., metadata={...})`.

Metadata is powerful but has a cost: by default it is included in the text sent to the embedding model and to the LLM. That helps when it adds meaning (a title or section name) and hurts when it is noise (file sizes, internal ids). Control it per document:

- `excluded_embed_metadata_keys=["file_size"]`: not used for embeddings.
- `excluded_llm_metadata_keys=["internal_id"]`: not shown to the LLM.

`node.get_content(metadata_mode=MetadataMode.LLM)` shows exactly what the LLM will see, which is the quickest way to check it.

Good metadata to add: title, section, source URL, date, product, language and access level. It enables citations and filters later.
concepts.code:
from llama_index.core import Document
from llama_index.core.schema import MetadataMode
from llama_index.core.node_parser import SentenceSplitter

doc = Document(
    text="Employees get 25 days of paid leave per year. Unused days expire in March.",
    metadata={"title": "Leave policy", "department": "hr", "internal_id": "HR-17"},
    excluded_llm_metadata_keys=["internal_id"],     # hide from the LLM
    excluded_embed_metadata_keys=["internal_id"],   # and from embeddings
)
nodes = SentenceSplitter().get_nodes_from_documents([doc])
print(len(nodes))                                   # 1 (short text, one chunk)
print(nodes[0].metadata["title"], nodes[0].ref_doc_id == doc.doc_id)   # Leave policy True
print(nodes[0].get_content(metadata_mode=MetadataMode.LLM))
# title: Leave policy
# department: hr
#
# Employees get 25 days of paid leave per year. Unused days expire in March.
takeaways: Documents are whole sources; nodes are the chunks that get retrieved
Nodes inherit metadata and link back to their document
Exclude noisy metadata from embeddings or the LLM
pitfalls: Stuffing long metadata (like full JSON records) into every node, which crowds out the real text in embeddings and prompts.

quiz.q: What is the unit that LlamaIndex embeds and retrieves?
quiz.explain: Documents are split into nodes; each node is embedded and retrieved separately.

concepts.name: Chunking with node parsers
concepts.summary: Split documents into nodes with SentenceSplitter and structure-aware splitters, and choose chunk size and overlap.
concepts.why: Chunking is one of the biggest levers on RAG quality, and the defaults are rarely optimal for your data.
concepts.body:
A **node parser** (or text splitter) cuts documents into nodes. The default is **`SentenceSplitter`**: it fills chunks up to `chunk_size` tokens (1024 by default) while trying not to break sentences, and repeats `chunk_overlap` tokens (200 by default) between neighbouring chunks so an idea cut at a boundary is not lost.

```python
splitter = SentenceSplitter(chunk_size=512, chunk_overlap=50)
nodes = splitter.get_nodes_from_documents(documents)
```

To use it during indexing, pass it as a **transformation** (any processing step applied while building the index): `VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(docs, transformations=[splitter])`.

Choosing a size:

- Small chunks (around 128 to 256 tokens) match precise questions well but may lack context.
- Large chunks (around 1024) carry more context but mix topics, which blurs their embeddings and costs more prompt tokens.
- Start near 512, then measure retrieval on real questions and adjust.

Node parsers that follow the document's structure often beat plain splitting:

- `MarkdownNodeParser` splits on headings and records the heading path in metadata.
- `CodeSplitter` splits program code along its structure, such as functions and classes.
- `SentenceWindowNodeParser` and `HierarchicalNodeParser` support advanced retrieval tricks (an Expert lesson).
- `SemanticSplitterNodeParser` splits where the meaning changes, using embeddings.

Node parsers can be chained: Markdown sections first, then `SentenceSplitter` for sections that are still too long. Whatever you choose, keep useful metadata (title, heading) on every node, because a chunk without context is hard to retrieve.
concepts.code:
from llama_index.core import Document
from llama_index.core.node_parser import MarkdownNodeParser, SentenceSplitter

md = Document(text="# Billing\n## Refunds\nRefunds take 5 days.\n## Invoices\nInvoices are PDFs.")

sections = MarkdownNodeParser().get_nodes_from_documents([md])
for n in sections:
    print(n.metadata.get("header_path"), "|", n.text.splitlines()[0])
# / | # Billing
# /Billing/ | ## Refunds
# /Billing/ | ## Invoices

splitter = SentenceSplitter(chunk_size=512, chunk_overlap=50)
long_doc = Document(text="A sentence about refunds. " * 400)
nodes = splitter.get_nodes_from_documents([long_doc])
print(len(nodes), len(nodes[0].text.split()))      # 6 340  (6 chunks, ~340 words each)

# During indexing:
# index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(docs, transformations=[splitter])
takeaways: `SentenceSplitter` defaults: chunk_size 1024, overlap 200 tokens
Pass node parsers as `transformations` when building an index
Structure-aware node parsers (Markdown, code) keep sections intact
pitfalls: Picking a chunk size once by intuition and never measuring retrieval quality on real questions.

quiz.q: Why do chunks overlap a little?
options: So an idea split across a boundary still appears whole in at least one chunk
quiz.explain: Overlap repeats some text between neighbours so boundary-crossing content is not lost.

concepts.name: VectorStoreIndex
concepts.summary: Build a VectorStoreIndex from documents or nodes, add and delete content, and understand what it stores.
concepts.why: The vector index is the default and most-used index in LlamaIndex; everything else builds on it.
concepts.body:
An **index** is your nodes organised so they can be searched quickly. The most common is **`VectorStoreIndex`**: it stores an embedding for every node and finds the nodes whose embeddings are closest to the question's embedding.

Two ways to build one:

```python
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(documents)   # parses into nodes for you
index = VectorStoreIndex(nodes)                      # when you already have nodes
```

Building calls the embedding model once per node (sending several at a time), so large collections take time and money. `show_progress=True` displays a progress bar.

By default the vectors live in memory in a `SimpleVectorStore`. For anything that must outlive the program, or is large, you plug in a real vector database (a later lesson). Alongside vectors, the index keeps a **docstore** (the node texts and metadata) and an **index store** (bookkeeping about which nodes it holds). A `StorageContext` groups all three.

Keeping it up to date:

- `index.insert(document)` adds a new document.
- `index.delete_ref_doc(doc_id, delete_from_docstore=True)` removes all nodes of a document.
- `index.refresh_ref_docs(documents)` re-indexes only documents whose text changed, which is why stable document ids matter.

From one index you create the objects you use day to day: `as_retriever()` gives a **retriever** (search only, no answer writing), `as_query_engine()` a query engine for answers, and `as_chat_engine()` a **chat engine** for conversations.

Other index types exist, such as `SummaryIndex` (reads every node, good for summarising a small set) and `PropertyGraphIndex` (stores facts as a network of linked things, a knowledge graph), but start with the vector index.
concepts.code:
from llama_index.core import Document, VectorStoreIndex

docs = [
    Document(text="Refunds take 5 business days.", id_="faq-refunds"),
    Document(text="Shipping is free over 50 EUR.", id_="faq-shipping"),
]
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(docs, show_progress=True)

index.insert(Document(text="Support is open Mon-Fri.", id_="faq-support"))
print(len(index.docstore.docs))                         # 3 nodes

index.delete_ref_doc("faq-shipping", delete_from_docstore=True)
print(len(index.docstore.docs))                         # 2

changed = index.refresh_ref_docs([Document(text="Refunds take 3 business days.", id_="faq-refunds")])
print(changed)                                          # [True]  (text changed, re-indexed)

retriever = index.as_retriever(similarity_top_k=1)
print(retriever.retrieve("money back")[0].node.text)   # Refunds take 3 business days.
takeaways: `VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(docs)` or `VectorStoreIndex(nodes)`
Insert, delete and refresh documents by stable ids
Create retrievers, query engines and chat engines from the index
pitfalls: Rebuilding the whole index from scratch on every change instead of inserting or refreshing changed documents.

quiz.q: What does refresh_ref_docs do with a document whose text is unchanged?
options: Skips it, re-indexing only changed documents
quiz.explain: It compares document content by id and only re-processes documents that changed.

concepts.name: Query engines and responses
concepts.summary: Configure as_query_engine (top-k, response mode, streaming) and read answers, sources and metadata from the Response.
concepts.why: The query engine is the main interface for question answering over your data.
concepts.body:
A **query engine** takes a question and returns an answer. `index.as_query_engine()` builds one from two parts:

- a **retriever** that finds relevant nodes, and
- a **response synthesizer** that sends them with the question to the LLM.

Common options:

- `similarity_top_k=4`: how many nodes to retrieve (default 2). More gives the LLM more context but costs tokens and can add noise.
- `response_mode="compact"`: the **response mode**, meaning how nodes are fitted into prompts to produce an answer (the default; a later lesson compares modes).
- `streaming=True`: send the answer piece by piece as the LLM writes it (**streaming**), instead of all at the end.
- `filters=...`: only search nodes with certain metadata (a later lesson).
- `llm=...`: use a different LLM for this engine.

The result of `query_engine.query("...")` is a **Response**:

- `str(response)` or `response.response`: the answer text.
- `response.source_nodes`: a list of `NodeWithScore`, the retrieved nodes with similarity scores. Use them to show citations ("Source: refunds.md").
- `response.metadata`: metadata of the source nodes by id.

With `streaming=True` you get a streaming response: iterate `response.response_gen` for text pieces, or call `response.print_response_stream()`.

The default prompt tells the LLM to answer from the context and not from prior knowledge. Even so, check answers against sources for important uses, and consider telling users when no relevant source was found.
concepts.code:
from llama_index.core import Document, VectorStoreIndex

index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents([
    Document(text="Refunds take 5 business days.", metadata={"source": "faq.md"}),
    Document(text="Our office is in Oslo.", metadata={"source": "about.md"}),
])
qe = index.as_query_engine(similarity_top_k=2)

response = qe.query("How long do refunds take?")
print(response.response)                     # Refunds take 5 business days.
for n in response.source_nodes:
    print(f"{n.score:.2f}", n.node.metadata["source"])
# 0.86 faq.md
# 0.72 about.md

streaming_qe = index.as_query_engine(streaming=True)
stream = streaming_qe.query("Where is the office?")
for piece in stream.response_gen:            # text arrives piece by piece
    print(piece, end="", flush=True)         # The office is in Oslo.
takeaways: `as_query_engine(similarity_top_k=..., streaming=...)` configures retrieval and output
Response: `.response` text plus `.source_nodes` with scores
Use source metadata for citations
pitfalls: Raising similarity_top_k to 20 to "be safe", which adds noise and cost and can make answers worse.

quiz.q: What are the two main parts of a default query engine?
options: A retriever and a response synthesizer
quiz.explain: The retriever finds nodes; the synthesizer turns nodes plus question into an answer with the LLM.

concepts.name: Saving and loading indexes
concepts.summary: Save an index to disk with storage_context.persist and load it back with load_index_from_storage.
concepts.why: Re-embedding every document on each start is slow and costs money; persistence avoids it.
concepts.body:
An in-memory index disappears when your program exits. Keeping data after the program stops is called **persistence**. Rebuilding it means embedding every chunk again, which is slow and costs money with paid embedding APIs.

**Save** it to a folder:

```python
index.storage_context.persist(persist_dir="storage")
```

This writes JSON files for the vectors, the docstore (node texts and metadata) and the index store.

**Load** it later:

```python
storage_context = StorageContext.from_defaults(persist_dir="storage")
index = load_index_from_storage(storage_context)
```

A common pattern is "build once, load afterwards": check whether the folder exists, and only build the index if it doesn't.

Things to watch:

- The embedding model is **not** saved. Set the same `Settings.embed_model` before loading, or queries will be compared against vectors from a different model.
- The default stores are JSON files loaded fully into memory. That is fine for thousands of chunks but not for millions.
- If the original files change, you need to update the index (insert, delete, refresh) and persist again.

For larger or shared data, use a **vector database** integration instead (Chroma, Qdrant, pgvector, Pinecone and many others). Those store vectors themselves, so you reconnect to them rather than loading files; a later lesson covers it.
concepts.code:
import os
from llama_index.core import (SimpleDirectoryReader, StorageContext, VectorStoreIndex,
                              load_index_from_storage)

PERSIST_DIR = "storage"

if not os.path.exists(PERSIST_DIR):
    documents = SimpleDirectoryReader("data").load_data()
    index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(documents)       # embeds everything once
    index.storage_context.persist(persist_dir=PERSIST_DIR)
    print("built and saved")
else:
    storage_context = StorageContext.from_defaults(persist_dir=PERSIST_DIR)
    index = load_index_from_storage(storage_context)          # no re-embedding
    print("loaded from disk")

print(index.as_query_engine().query("How long do refunds take?"))
takeaways: `index.storage_context.persist(persist_dir=...)` saves to disk
`load_index_from_storage(StorageContext.from_defaults(persist_dir=...))` loads it
Set the same embedding model before loading
pitfalls: Loading a saved index with a different Settings.embed_model than the one used to build it.

quiz.q: What is NOT saved by storage_context.persist()?
quiz.explain: Only data is persisted; you must configure the same embedding model again before querying.

concepts.name: Chat engines
concepts.summary: Hold multi-turn conversations over your data with as_chat_engine and the condense_plus_context mode.
concepts.why: Users ask follow-up questions like "and for Germany?"; a chat engine remembers what they mean.
concepts.body:
A query engine treats every question on its own. A **chat engine** keeps the conversation history, so follow-ups work:

```python
chat_engine = index.as_chat_engine(chat_mode="condense_plus_context")
chat_engine.chat("What is the refund period?")
chat_engine.chat("Does that apply to sale items too?")
```

The second question only makes sense with the first. The **`condense_plus_context`** mode handles this in two steps:

1. It asks the LLM to rewrite ("condense") the latest message plus history into a standalone question, such as "Does the refund period apply to sale items?".
2. It retrieves context for that question and answers with the history and the context.

Other modes:

- `context`: retrieves using the raw latest message, then answers with history. Simpler, weaker on follow-ups.
- `condense_question`: rewrites the question and runs a query engine, without history in the final answer.
- `simple`: plain chat with the LLM, no retrieval.

Useful methods:

- `chat(msg)` returns a response with `.response` and `.source_nodes`.
- `stream_chat(msg)` streams tokens through `.response_gen`.
- `reset()` clears the history.
- `chat_history` shows the stored messages.

History is kept in a memory object with a token limit, so very long conversations drop their oldest turns. A chat engine object holds one conversation, so in an app with many users, create or restore one per conversation; never share one engine between users.

For conversations that also need tools or several data sources, use an agent instead (a later lesson).
concepts.code:
from llama_index.core import Document, VectorStoreIndex

index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents([
    Document(text="Refunds are possible within 30 days of delivery."),
    Document(text="Sale items can be refunded within 14 days only."),
])
chat = index.as_chat_engine(chat_mode="condense_plus_context",
                            system_prompt="You answer questions about our shop policies.")

print(chat.chat("What is the refund period?").response)
# You can request a refund within 30 days of delivery.
print(chat.chat("And for items bought on sale?").response)
# Sale items can only be refunded within 14 days.
print(len(chat.chat_history))     # 4 messages (2 user, 2 assistant)

chat.reset()                      # start a fresh conversation
takeaways: Chat engines keep history so follow-up questions work
`condense_plus_context` rewrites the question, then retrieves and answers
One chat engine per conversation; `reset()` clears history
pitfalls: Sharing one chat engine instance across all users of an app, so they see each other's conversation context.

quiz.q: In condense_plus_context mode, why is the question rewritten first?
options: So retrieval uses a standalone question that includes what the follow-up refers to
quiz.explain: A follow-up like 'and for sale items?' retrieves poorly; the rewrite adds the missing context.

concepts.name: Retrievers and custom query engines
concepts.summary: Use retrievers directly, inspect NodeWithScore results, and assemble a RetrieverQueryEngine with postprocessors.
concepts.why: Separating retrieval from answering lets you test, tune and reuse each part on its own.
concepts.body:
A **retriever** does only the search half: question in, ranked nodes out. Get one from an index:

```python
retriever = index.as_retriever(similarity_top_k=5)
results = retriever.retrieve("refund for damaged items")
```

Each result is a **`NodeWithScore`**: `.node` (text, metadata, id) and `.score` (how similar it is; higher is closer for most vector stores). Testing retrievers directly, without an LLM, is fast and cheap, and is the best way to tune chunking and `similarity_top_k`.

You can build a query engine from explicit parts with **`RetrieverQueryEngine`**:

```python
query_engine = RetrieverQueryEngine.from_args(
    retriever,
    node_postprocessors=[SimilarityPostprocessor(similarity_cutoff=0.75)],
    response_mode="compact",
)
```

**Node postprocessors** are steps that run between retrieval and the LLM. They can drop, reorder or change nodes:

- `SimilarityPostprocessor(similarity_cutoff=...)` drops weak matches.
- `KeywordNodePostprocessor` keeps or removes nodes containing given words.
- Rerankers re-score nodes with a stronger model (an Advanced lesson).

Score scales depend on the embedding model and vector store, so pick a cutoff by looking at real scores for good and bad matches, not by guessing.

Because retrievers share one interface, you can swap in other kinds (keyword search, hybrid search, choosing between indexes) without changing the rest of your pipeline. Agents can also use a retriever wrapped as a tool.
concepts.code:
from llama_index.core import Document, VectorStoreIndex
from llama_index.core.postprocessor import SimilarityPostprocessor
from llama_index.core.query_engine import RetrieverQueryEngine

index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents([
    Document(text="Damaged items are refunded in full."),
    Document(text="Gift cards cannot be refunded."),
    Document(text="Our office dog is called Biscuit."),
])
retriever = index.as_retriever(similarity_top_k=3)

for r in retriever.retrieve("refund for a broken product"):
    print(f"{r.score:.2f}  {r.node.text}")
# 0.84  Damaged items are refunded in full.
# 0.77  Gift cards cannot be refunded.
# 0.61  Our office dog is called Biscuit.

qe = RetrieverQueryEngine.from_args(
    retriever, node_postprocessors=[SimilarityPostprocessor(similarity_cutoff=0.7)])
resp = qe.query("Can I get a refund for a broken product?")
print(len(resp.source_nodes))     # 2  (the dog was filtered out)
takeaways: `as_retriever(similarity_top_k=k).retrieve(q)` returns NodeWithScore list
`RetrieverQueryEngine.from_args(retriever, node_postprocessors=[...])`
Tune retrieval on its own before touching prompts
pitfalls: Choosing a similarity_cutoff without looking at actual score distributions, which silently filters out every result.

quiz.q: Why test a retriever on its own, without the LLM?
options: It is fast and cheap and shows whether the right nodes are found, separately from answer writing
quiz.explain: Isolating retrieval shows if failures come from search or from answer generation.

concepts.name: Metadata filters
concepts.summary: Restrict retrieval to nodes whose metadata matches conditions, using MetadataFilters and FilterOperator.
concepts.why: Filters enforce hard constraints such as year, product or user permissions that similarity search alone can't.
concepts.body:
Similarity search finds text that *sounds* related. It can't guarantee hard conditions like "only 2025 documents" or "only documents this user may see". **Metadata filters** add those conditions to the search.

```python
filters = MetadataFilters(filters=[
    MetadataFilter(key="department", value="hr"),
    MetadataFilter(key="year", value=2024, operator=FilterOperator.GTE),
])
retriever = index.as_retriever(filters=filters, similarity_top_k=3)
```

- `MetadataFilter(key, value, operator)`: the default operator is equality. Others include `NE`, `GT`, `GTE`, `LT`, `LTE`, `IN`, `NIN` (not in) and `TEXT_MATCH`.
- `MetadataFilters(filters=[...], condition="and")`: combine with `"and"` (default) or `"or"`. Filter groups can be nested.

The same `filters=` argument works on `as_query_engine` and `as_chat_engine`.

Filters only work on metadata you stored, so plan it when you load your data: department, product, language, date as a number (such as `2025`) and access level.

Support for each operator depends on the vector store. The simple in-memory store and most popular databases handle the common ones, but check the integration's docs before relying on `TEXT_MATCH` or nested groups.

For **permissions**, filters are the right tool: add the user's allowed groups as a filter on every query. Never rely on the prompt ("don't reveal HR documents"); a filter makes sure such nodes are never retrieved at all.

When the filter comes from the user's question ("reports from 2023"), an LLM can pull it out, but check that the values are allowed before using them.
concepts.code:
from llama_index.core import Document, VectorStoreIndex
from llama_index.core.vector_stores import FilterOperator, MetadataFilter, MetadataFilters

index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents([
    Document(text="2023 HR handbook: 20 leave days.", metadata={"dept": "hr", "year": 2023}),
    Document(text="2025 HR handbook: 25 leave days.", metadata={"dept": "hr", "year": 2025}),
    Document(text="2025 sales targets.", metadata={"dept": "sales", "year": 2025}),
])

filters = MetadataFilters(filters=[
    MetadataFilter(key="dept", value="hr"),                                # equality
    MetadataFilter(key="year", value=2024, operator=FilterOperator.GTE),
])
for r in index.as_retriever(filters=filters, similarity_top_k=5).retrieve("leave days"):
    print(r.node.metadata, r.node.text)
# {'dept': 'hr', 'year': 2025} 2025 HR handbook: 25 leave days.

qe = index.as_query_engine(filters=filters)    # same filters for answers
takeaways: `MetadataFilters([MetadataFilter(key, value, operator)])` restricts search
Works on retrievers, query engines and chat engines via `filters=`
Use filters, not prompts, for permissions
pitfalls: Storing years as strings like "2025" and then using GTE comparisons, which may compare text instead of numbers or fail.

quiz.q: How should you stop users from retrieving documents they are not allowed to see?
options: Tell the LLM in the system prompt not to reveal them
Apply a metadata filter with the user's allowed groups on every query
quiz.explain: Filters prevent restricted nodes from being retrieved at all; prompts can be ignored or bypassed.

concepts.name: Vector store integrations
concepts.summary: Store embeddings in a real vector database such as Chroma via StorageContext, and reconnect with from_vector_store.
concepts.why: A real RAG service needs storage that survives restarts, grows to millions of chunks and can be shared, instead of JSON files loaded into memory.
concepts.body:
A **vector store** is the database that holds embeddings and runs similarity search. LlamaIndex's default `SimpleVectorStore` keeps everything in memory. For real applications you use an integration, each in its own package: Chroma, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, Pinecone, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Postgres with pgvector, MongoDB Atlas, Redis and many more.

The pattern is the same for all of them:

1. Create the database connection object and the LlamaIndex vector store object.
2. Wrap it in a `StorageContext` and build the index with it:

```python
storage_context = StorageContext.from_defaults(vector_store=vector_store)
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(docs, storage_context=storage_context)
```

3. Later, reconnect without re-embedding:

```python
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_vector_store(vector_store)
```

Most of these databases also store the node text and metadata, so you don't need to persist a separate docstore.

How to choose:

- **Chroma** or **LanceDB**: embedded, file-based, easy for local work and small projects.
- **pgvector**: if you already run Postgres, keeps vectors next to your other data.
- **Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, Pinecone**: dedicated servers or hosted services for large collections, with strong filtering.

Check what each integration supports: metadata filter operators, hybrid search (exact-word matching plus vector search) and deletion by document id. The vector length (how many numbers each one has) is fixed by your embedding model, so changing models means creating a new collection.
concepts.code:
# pip install llama-index-vector-stores-chroma chromadb
import chromadb
from llama_index.core import Document, StorageContext, VectorStoreIndex
from llama_index.vector_stores.chroma import ChromaVectorStore

client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma_db")        # data saved on disk
collection = client.get_or_create_collection("handbook")
vector_store = ChromaVectorStore(chroma_collection=collection)

# First run: embed and store
storage_context = StorageContext.from_defaults(vector_store=vector_store)
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(
    [Document(text="Refunds take 5 days.", metadata={"dept": "support"})],
    storage_context=storage_context,
)

# Any later run (or another process): reconnect, no re-embedding
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_vector_store(vector_store)
print(index.as_retriever().retrieve("refund time")[0].node.text)   # Refunds take 5 days.
print(collection.count())                                          # 1
takeaways: Each vector database is a separate integration package
Build with `StorageContext.from_defaults(vector_store=...)`
Reconnect with `VectorStoreIndex.from_vector_store(vector_store)`
pitfalls: Calling from_documents on every application start against a persistent store, which inserts duplicate copies of every chunk.

quiz.q: Your Chroma collection already contains embedded documents. How do you get an index to query it?
quiz.explain: from_vector_store wraps the existing store without embedding anything again.

concepts.name: Response synthesis and prompts
concepts.summary: Choose response modes such as compact, refine and tree_summarize, and customise the QA prompt.
concepts.why: How retrieved text becomes an answer affects accuracy, cost and how well long contexts are handled.
concepts.body:
After retrieval, a **response synthesizer** turns the question plus nodes into an answer. The `response_mode` decides how:

- `compact` (default): packs as many nodes as fit into each prompt, then refines across prompts if needed. Few LLM calls.
- `refine`: one call per node; each call improves the previous answer with the next node. Thorough but slow and costly.
- `tree_summarize`: answers over groups of nodes, then summarises those answers, repeating until one remains. Good for summaries over many chunks.
- `simple_summarize`: truncates everything into one prompt. Cheap, may lose information.
- `accumulate`: answers separately per node and joins the results, useful for "list what each document says".
- `no_text`: retrieval only, no LLM call. Handy for testing.

Set it with `index.as_query_engine(response_mode="tree_summarize")` or build one with `get_response_synthesizer(response_mode=...)`.

**Custom prompts.** The main question-answering prompt is called `text_qa_template`. It receives `{context_str}` (the retrieved text) and `{query_str}` (the question). Replace it to change tone, language, citation style or the "I don't know" behaviour:

```python
qe.update_prompts({"response_synthesizer:text_qa_template": PromptTemplate(...)})
```

`qe.get_prompts()` lists every prompt key an engine uses.

Prompt rules that pay off: answer only from the context, say clearly when the context doesn't contain the answer, cite sources using metadata, and match the user's language.
concepts.code:
from llama_index.core import Document, PromptTemplate, VectorStoreIndex

index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents([
    Document(text="Refunds take 5 business days.", metadata={"source": "faq.md"}),
])
qe = index.as_query_engine(response_mode="compact", similarity_top_k=3)
print(list(qe.get_prompts()))
# ['response_synthesizer:text_qa_template', 'response_synthesizer:refine_template', ...]

qa = PromptTemplate(
    "Answer using ONLY the context below. If the answer is not there, reply "
    "'I could not find this in our documents.' Cite the source file.\n"
    "Context:\n{context_str}\n\nQuestion: {query_str}\nAnswer: "
)
qe.update_prompts({"response_synthesizer:text_qa_template": qa})
print(qe.query("Do you ship to Mars?"))       # I could not find this in our documents.

summary_qe = index.as_query_engine(response_mode="tree_summarize")
takeaways: `compact` (default), `refine`, `tree_summarize`, `accumulate`, `no_text`
`text_qa_template` uses `{context_str}` and `{query_str}`
Use `get_prompts()` and `update_prompts()` to inspect and replace prompts
pitfalls: Using refine mode with a high similarity_top_k, which makes one LLM call per node and multiplies cost and waiting time.

quiz.q: You need a summary of themes across 40 retrieved chunks. Which response mode fits best?
quiz.explain: tree_summarize builds the answer hierarchically over all chunks, suited to summaries.

concepts.name: Ingestion pipelines
concepts.summary: Run documents through an IngestionPipeline of transformations that skips unchanged work and writes to a vector store.
concepts.why: Repeatable, incremental ingestion (loading, chunking, embedding and storing your data) is what keeps a RAG index correct as source data changes.
concepts.body:
An **`IngestionPipeline`** applies a list of **transformations** to documents, in order, and can write the result straight to a vector store. Transformations include node parsers, metadata extractors and the embedding model itself.

```python
pipeline = IngestionPipeline(
    transformations=[SentenceSplitter(chunk_size=512), TitleExtractor(), embed_model],
    vector_store=vector_store,
    docstore=SimpleDocumentStore(),
)
pipeline.run(documents=documents)
```

Why use it instead of `from_documents`:

- **Caching.** Each transformation's output is saved, keyed by its input (a **cache**), so re-running on unchanged data skips the expensive steps.
- **De-duplication.** With a `docstore` attached, the pipeline remembers each document's id and content hash. Unchanged documents are skipped; changed ones are re-processed and their old nodes replaced (the default `upserts` strategy; an **upsert** updates an entry if it exists and inserts it if not). Stable document ids, such as from `filename_as_id=True`, make this work.
- **One place for your ingestion logic**, which you can run from a scheduled job.

**Metadata extractors** use an LLM to add metadata to nodes, for example `TitleExtractor`, `SummaryExtractor` or `QuestionsAnsweredExtractor`. They can improve retrieval but cost an LLM call per node, so use them where they measurably help.

Save the pipeline's cache and docstore with `pipeline.persist("./pipeline_storage")` and load them with `pipeline.load(...)` on the next run. `pipeline.run(..., num_workers=4)` works on four groups of documents at once.

After ingestion, query with `VectorStoreIndex.from_vector_store(vector_store)`.
concepts.code:
from llama_index.core import Document, Settings, VectorStoreIndex
from llama_index.core.ingestion import IngestionPipeline
from llama_index.core.node_parser import SentenceSplitter
from llama_index.core.storage.docstore import SimpleDocumentStore
import chromadb
from llama_index.vector_stores.chroma import ChromaVectorStore

collection = chromadb.EphemeralClient().get_or_create_collection("docs")   # in-memory demo
vector_store = ChromaVectorStore(chroma_collection=collection)   # or Qdrant, pgvector...
pipeline = IngestionPipeline(
    transformations=[SentenceSplitter(chunk_size=512, chunk_overlap=50),
                     Settings.embed_model],   # embedding is the last step
    docstore=SimpleDocumentStore(),          # enables de-duplication
    vector_store=vector_store,
)
docs = [Document(text="Refunds take 5 days.", id_="faq.md"),
        Document(text="Office in Oslo.", id_="about.md")]
print(len(pipeline.run(documents=docs)))    # 2 nodes processed
print(len(pipeline.run(documents=docs)))    # 0  (unchanged, skipped)

docs[0] = Document(text="Refunds take 3 days.", id_="faq.md")
print(len(pipeline.run(documents=docs)))    # 1  (only the changed doc)
pipeline.persist("./pipeline_storage")

index = VectorStoreIndex.from_vector_store(vector_store)
takeaways: Pipelines chain node parsers, metadata extractors and the embedding model
A docstore enables skipping unchanged documents and replacing changed ones
Persist cache and docstore between runs
pitfalls: Running a pipeline with a docstore but unstable document ids (new random ids on every load), so every run looks like new documents.

quiz.q: You re-run a pipeline (with a docstore) on 1,000 documents where only 3 changed. Roughly what gets re-processed?
options: Only new ones, never changed ones
quiz.explain: The docstore compares ids and content hashes and re-processes only changed or new documents.

concepts.name: Structured outputs
concepts.summary: Extract typed Pydantic objects with structured_predict, as_structured_llm and query engines with output_cls.
concepts.why: Extraction and classification over documents feed other code, which needs fields, not prose.
concepts.body:
Sometimes you want data, not an answer: invoice fields from a PDF, a category for a ticket, a list of action items from meeting notes. Describe the data as a **Pydantic** model and let LlamaIndex fill it. Pydantic is a popular library for describing data as a class with typed fields and checking real data against it.

Three ways in:

- **`llm.structured_predict(Model, prompt, **variables)`** formats a `PromptTemplate` and returns a `Model` instance. Good for one-off extraction.
- **`llm.as_structured_llm(Model)`** wraps an LLM so every chat or completion returns the model. The filled-in object is in `response.raw`.
- **`index.as_query_engine(output_cls=Model)`** runs RAG and returns a structured answer: `response.response` is the `Model` instance and `source_nodes` still shows the evidence.

Agents accept `output_cls=Model` too; read the result with `response.get_pydantic_model(Model)`.

Under the hood LlamaIndex uses the provider's function calling or JSON mode where available, and otherwise asks for JSON in the prompt and reads it out of the reply. Function-calling models (current OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini and many Ollama models) are most reliable.

Schema tips:

- Use descriptive field names and `Field(description=...)`; the model reads them.
- Use `Literal[...]` or enums for categories.
- Make fields optional when data may be missing, so the model isn't pushed to invent values.
- Keep schemas small; for long documents, extract per chunk and merge in code.
concepts.code:
from typing import Literal, Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from llama_index.core import PromptTemplate
from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI

class Invoice(BaseModel):
    vendor: str
    total: float = Field(description="Total amount including tax")
    currency: Literal["EUR", "USD", "GBP"]
    due_date: Optional[str] = Field(None, description="YYYY-MM-DD if stated")

llm = OpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0)
prompt = PromptTemplate("Extract the invoice details from:\n{text}")

inv = llm.structured_predict(Invoice, prompt, text="ACME Ltd. Total due: 1,210.00 EUR by 2026-11-30.")
print(inv)        # vendor='ACME Ltd.' total=1210.0 currency='EUR' due_date='2026-11-30'

sllm = llm.as_structured_llm(Invoice)
resp = sllm.complete("Bill from Globex, 99 USD, no due date.")
print(resp.raw.vendor, resp.raw.due_date)    # Globex None

# RAG + structure: index.as_query_engine(output_cls=Invoice).query("...").response
takeaways: `structured_predict(Model, prompt, **vars)` for one-off extraction
`as_structured_llm(Model)` makes every call return the model (in `.raw`)
`as_query_engine(output_cls=Model)` adds structure to RAG answers
pitfalls: Making every field required when source documents often lack some values, which encourages the model to make them up.

quiz.q: Where is the Pydantic object when you call a structured LLM's complete()?
quiz.explain: A structured LLM returns the parsed model instance in the response's raw attribute.

concepts.name: Agents with FunctionAgent
concepts.summary: Build a tool-using FunctionAgent from Python functions and query engine tools, and run it with async (asynchronous) code.
concepts.why: Agents can pick between several data sources and tools per question, which a fixed query engine can't.
concepts.body:
An agent is an LLM in a loop: it reads the request, decides which tool to call, looks at the result and repeats until it can answer. In LlamaIndex the standard agent is **`FunctionAgent`**, which uses the model's tool (function) calling:

```python
agent = FunctionAgent(tools=[multiply, search_docs], llm=OpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini"),
                      system_prompt="You are a helpful assistant.")
response = await agent.run("What is 7 * 8, and what does the handbook say about leave?")
```

**Tools.** A plain Python function becomes a tool automatically: its name, type hints and docstring tell the model what it does, so write the docstring for the model. `FunctionTool.from_defaults(fn, name=..., description=...)` gives more control. **`QueryEngineTool.from_defaults(query_engine, name=..., description=...)`** turns a whole RAG pipeline into one tool. That is how an agent can choose between, say, an HR index and a product index.

**Async.** `agent.run(...)` is **asynchronous**: `async`/`await` is Python's way of running code that waits for slow things (like model calls) without freezing everything else. In practice: put your calls inside an `async def main():`, write `await` before `agent.run(...)`, and start it with `asyncio.run(main())`. In a Jupyter **notebook** (an interactive document that runs Python in cells) you can use `await` directly.

**Other agent types.** `ReActAgent` works with models that lack native tool calling, by reasoning in text. `CodeActAgent` writes and runs code as its actions, which needs a **sandbox**: a locked-down space where that code can't harm your system.

Older APIs such as `OpenAIAgent`, `AgentRunner` and `ReActAgent.from_tools` are legacy; use the workflow-based agents.
concepts.code:
import asyncio
from llama_index.core import Document, VectorStoreIndex
from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import FunctionAgent
from llama_index.core.tools import QueryEngineTool
from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI

def multiply(a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """Multiply two numbers."""
    return a * b

hr_index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents([Document(text="Staff get 25 leave days a year.")])
hr_tool = QueryEngineTool.from_defaults(
    hr_index.as_query_engine(), name="hr_handbook",
    description="Answers questions about HR policies such as leave and benefits.")

agent = FunctionAgent(tools=[multiply, hr_tool], llm=OpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini"),
                      system_prompt="Use tools for facts and arithmetic.")

async def main():
    response = await agent.run("How many leave days do 3 employees get in total?")
    print(str(response))        # 3 employees get 75 leave days in total.

asyncio.run(main())
takeaways: `FunctionAgent(tools, llm, system_prompt)` runs a tool-calling loop
Functions become tools via name, type hints and docstring; QueryEngineTool wraps RAG
`await agent.run(...)` inside `async def`, started with `asyncio.run`
pitfalls: Calling agent.run(...) without await in normal code and printing a handler object instead of the answer.

quiz.q: You have separate indexes for HR policies and product manuals. How can one agent use both?
options: Wrap each query engine in a QueryEngineTool with a clear description
quiz.explain: Each QueryEngineTool is a tool; the agent picks the right one from its name and description.

concepts.name: Parsing complex documents with LlamaParse
concepts.summary: Know when to use LlamaIndex's hosted LlamaParse platform for PDFs with tables and layouts, and how to call it.
concepts.why: Bad parsing (turning a file into clean text) of tables and multi-column PDFs is a common hidden cause of wrong RAG answers.
concepts.body:
Simple PDF readers extract text in reading order and often scramble tables, multi-column pages, charts and scanned pages. The RAG system then retrieves garbled chunks, and answers suffer.

**LlamaParse** is LlamaIndex's hosted document platform. Its docs present several products under one API key:

- **Parse**: converts PDFs, scans and Office files into clean Markdown or JSON, including tables.
- **Extract**: pulls fields matching a schema you define.
- **Classify** and **Split**: sort documents by type and split combined files.
- **Index**: hosted loading, embedding and retrieval for RAG.

Older material calls the platform **LlamaCloud** and uses the `llama-parse` or `llama-cloud-services` packages; the current Python SDK is `llama-cloud`, imported as `llama_cloud`, and reads the `LLAMA_CLOUD_API_KEY` environment variable. Parse and Extract have moved to a v2 API, so check the docs for current parameters. It is a paid service with a free allowance; pricing changes, so check the website.

When to use it:

- Many tables, forms, financial reports, slides or scanned pages.
- When parsed text from `SimpleDirectoryReader` looks wrong on inspection.

When not to: plain text, Markdown or simple PDFs parse fine locally and for free. Also check data policies, because documents are uploaded to a third party.

Whatever parser you use, print a few parsed pages before indexing. Five minutes of looking at parser output can save days of prompt tuning.

The Markdown output works well with `MarkdownNodeParser`, which keeps table and section structure together.
concepts.code:
# pip install llama-cloud ; export LLAMA_CLOUD_API_KEY=llx-...
from llama_cloud import LlamaCloud
from llama_index.core import Document

client = LlamaCloud()                                   # reads LLAMA_CLOUD_API_KEY
file = client.files.create(file="annual_report.pdf", purpose="parse")
result = client.parsing.parse(
    file_id=file.id,
    tier="agentic",                                     # parsing quality tier
    version="latest",
    expand=["markdown"],
)
pages = [p.markdown for p in result.markdown.pages]
print(pages[0][:200])                                   # | Quarter | Revenue | ... (tables as Markdown)

docs = [Document(text=md, metadata={"file_name": "annual_report.pdf", "page": i + 1})
        for i, md in enumerate(pages)]
# then: MarkdownNodeParser / SentenceSplitter -> VectorStoreIndex
takeaways: LlamaParse parses complex PDFs, tables and scans into Markdown/JSON
Current SDK: `llama-cloud` with `LLAMA_CLOUD_API_KEY`; older docs say LlamaCloud/llama-parse
Inspect parsed output before indexing, whatever parser you use
pitfalls: Uploading confidential documents to a hosted parser without checking your organisation's data policy.

quiz.q: Answers about numbers in financial-report tables are often wrong, and the parsed text shows table cells jumbled into one line. What is the best first fix?
options: Use a layout-aware parser such as LlamaParse and check its output
quiz.explain: The retrieval input is broken at the parsing stage; better parsing fixes the root cause.

concepts.name: Agent memory, state and streaming
concepts.summary: Keep conversations with Context, store state, save it between requests, and stream agent events.
concepts.why: Real assistants must remember the conversation, survive across web requests and show progress while working.
concepts.body:
By default each `agent.run(...)` call starts fresh. To keep a conversation, pass a **`Context`**:

```python
ctx = Context(agent)
await agent.run("My name is Ana.", ctx=ctx)
await agent.run("What's my name?", ctx=ctx)   # remembers: Ana
```

The context holds the chat memory and a **store** of arbitrary state. Read and write it with `await ctx.store.get("key", default=None)` and `await ctx.store.set("key", value)`. Tools can receive the context too: add a parameter typed `ctx: Context` and LlamaIndex passes it in, so a tool can update state such as a shopping cart.

**Between web requests**, turn the context into a plain dictionary with `ctx.to_dict()`, save it (for example in a database), and rebuild it later with `Context.from_dict(agent, data)`. Values in the store must be serialisable: convertible to JSON-like data that can be saved and read back.

Long conversations are trimmed by the agent's memory to fit a token limit. For control, pass a `Memory` object (`from llama_index.core.memory import Memory`), which supports a short-term token limit plus long-term memory blocks such as extracted facts.

**Streaming.** `agent.run(...)` returns a handler. Iterate its events before awaiting the result:

```python
handler = agent.run("...", ctx=ctx)
async for ev in handler.stream_events():
    ...
response = await handler
```

Useful event types: `AgentStream` (`ev.delta` is new text), `ToolCall` and `ToolCallResult` (`ev.tool_name`, `ev.tool_kwargs`, `ev.tool_output`). Show tool activity in your interface; users trust agents more when they can see what was looked up.
concepts.code:
import asyncio
from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import AgentStream, FunctionAgent, ToolCallResult
from llama_index.core.workflow import Context
from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI
async def add_to_cart(ctx: Context, item: str) -> str:
    """Add an item to the user's shopping cart."""
    cart = await ctx.store.get("cart", default=[])
    cart.append(item)
    await ctx.store.set("cart", cart)
    return f"Cart now has: {', '.join(cart)}"

agent = FunctionAgent(tools=[add_to_cart], llm=OpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini"))

async def main():
    ctx = Context(agent)
    handler = agent.run("Add apples and bread to my cart.", ctx=ctx)
    async for ev in handler.stream_events():
        if isinstance(ev, ToolCallResult):
            print(f"[tool] {ev.tool_name}({ev.tool_kwargs}) -> {ev.tool_output}")
        elif isinstance(ev, AgentStream): print(ev.delta, end="", flush=True)
    await handler
    ctx2 = Context.from_dict(agent, ctx.to_dict())         # e.g. saved between requests
    print("\n", await ctx2.store.get("cart", default=[]))             # ['apples', 'bread']

asyncio.run(main())
takeaways: Pass the same `Context` to keep conversation and state
`ctx.store.get/set` (awaited) for state; tools can take `ctx: Context`
`ctx.to_dict()` / `Context.from_dict()` across requests; stream with `stream_events()`
pitfalls: Creating a new Context on every web request and wondering why the agent forgets the conversation.

quiz.q: How do you continue a conversation in a later HTTP request handled by another server process?
options: Save ctx.to_dict() and rebuild with Context.from_dict(agent, data)
quiz.explain: Serialising the context preserves memory and state so another process can restore it.

concepts.name: Workflows: steps and events
concepts.summary: Write Workflows whose @step methods react to custom Events, with StartEvent/StopEvent and shared Context state.
concepts.why: Workflows are how LlamaIndex expresses any multi-step AI program, including its own agents, with full control.
concepts.body:
A **Workflow** is a class whose async methods, marked with `@step`, react to **events**. An event is a small typed message, a Pydantic class you define by subclassing `Event`.

The type hints define the wiring:

```python
@step
async def draft(self, ev: StartEvent) -> DraftEvent: ...
@step
async def review(self, ev: DraftEvent) -> StopEvent: ...
```

- `StartEvent` carries the keyword arguments given to `run(...)`: `ev.topic`, or `ev.get("topic")` when it may be missing.
- A step returning `DraftEvent` triggers every step that accepts `DraftEvent`.
- Returning `StopEvent(result=...)` ends the run; `await workflow.run(...)` gives you that result.

LlamaIndex checks the wiring before running, so a step whose event nothing produces is caught early.

Patterns:

- **Branching**: return different event types from one step (annotate the return as `EventA | EventB`).
- **Loops**: return an event handled by an earlier step, for example a retry after a failed check. Keep a counter.
- **Parallel work**: `ctx.send_event(...)` several times, and collect results with `ctx.collect_events(ev, [ResultEvent] * n)`.
- **Shared state**: add `ctx: Context` to a step and use `await ctx.store.get/set`.
- **Progress**: `ctx.write_event_to_stream(ev)` sends events to `handler.stream_events()`.

Set `timeout=` (seconds) when creating the workflow to stop runaway runs. Workflows are also published as the standalone `llama-index-workflows` package (imported as `workflows`); inside LlamaIndex use `llama_index.core.workflow`.

Use a workflow when the steps are known (classify, retrieve, check, answer); use an agent when the LLM should choose the steps. Agents themselves are workflows, so they can be called from a step.
takeaways: `@step` methods consume and return typed Events; type hints define the wiring
`StartEvent` holds run() arguments; `StopEvent(result=...)` ends the run
Use `ctx.store` for state and `timeout=` to bound runs
pitfalls: Returning an event type that no step accepts, which LlamaIndex's wiring check reports before the run starts.

quiz.q: What starts a step annotated as async def review(self, ev: DraftEvent) -> StopEvent?
quiz.explain: Steps are triggered by events of the type they accept; returning DraftEvent anywhere triggers review.

concepts.name: Multi-agent systems with AgentWorkflow
concepts.summary: Coordinate several specialised agents with AgentWorkflow handoffs, shared state, or an orchestrator agent.
concepts.why: Splitting a complex job across focused agents keeps each prompt and tool set small and reliable.
concepts.body:
One agent with twenty tools and a giant system prompt gets confused. Splitting the job across **several specialised agents**, each with a few tools and a narrow role, usually works better.

**`AgentWorkflow`** is the built-in way to do this with **handoffs**, where one agent passes control of the conversation to another:

```python
research = FunctionAgent(name="researcher", description="Finds facts with web search",
                         tools=[search], can_handoff_to=["writer"], llm=llm)
writer = FunctionAgent(name="writer", description="Writes the final report", llm=llm)
workflow = AgentWorkflow(agents=[research, writer], root_agent="researcher")
response = await workflow.run(user_msg="Write a short report on heat pumps.")
```

- Every agent needs a unique `name` and a `description`; other agents read the description when deciding whom to hand off to.
- `can_handoff_to` limits who an agent may pass control to.
- `root_agent` receives the user's message first.
- `initial_state={...}` creates shared state that tools can read and write through `ctx.store`, for example research notes the writer later uses.

Only one agent is active at a time; a handoff passes the conversation along.

Other patterns:

- **Orchestrator**: one top-level agent calls other agents *as tools* (wrap each sub-agent's `run` in an async function). The orchestrator keeps control and decides when to finish.
- **Custom workflow**: write a `Workflow` that calls agents in a fixed order or in parallel. Most predictable.

Stream events to watch handoffs: `AgentOutput` and the `current_agent_name` field on events show which agent is speaking. Multi-agent runs make many LLM calls, so measure cost and use simpler designs when they suffice.
concepts.code:
import asyncio
from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import AgentWorkflow, FunctionAgent
from llama_index.core.workflow import Context
from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI

llm = OpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini")
async def save_note(ctx: Context, note: str) -> str:
    """Save a research note for the writer."""
    state = await ctx.store.get("state")
    state["notes"].append(note)
    await ctx.store.set("state", state)
    return "saved"

researcher = FunctionAgent(name="researcher", description="Collects key facts as notes.",
    system_prompt="Save 3 short facts with save_note, then hand off to writer.",
    tools=[save_note], llm=llm, can_handoff_to=["writer"])
writer = FunctionAgent(name="writer", description="Writes the final answer from notes.",
    system_prompt="Write a 3-sentence summary from the saved notes in state.",
    tools=[], llm=llm)

workflow = AgentWorkflow(agents=[researcher, writer], root_agent="researcher",
                         initial_state={"notes": []})
async def main():
    print(await workflow.run(user_msg="Summarize why heat pumps are efficient."))
asyncio.run(main())
takeaways: `AgentWorkflow(agents, root_agent)` coordinates agents through handoffs
Names, descriptions and `can_handoff_to` steer who gets control
Shared `initial_state` lets agents pass data via `ctx.store`
pitfalls: Writing vague agent descriptions, so agents hand off to the wrong colleague or never hand off.

quiz.q: What do agents use to decide which other agent to hand off to?
options: The other agents' names and descriptions
The order of the agents list only
quiz.explain: Handoff decisions are made by the LLM from the available agents' names and descriptions.

concepts.name: Reranking and hybrid search
concepts.summary: Improve retrieval precision with rerankers and recall with hybrid BM25 + vector search fused by QueryFusionRetriever.
concepts.why: These two techniques give some of the largest, most reliable quality gains in real-world RAG.
concepts.body:
Plain vector search has two common weaknesses. Its top results are often *roughly* related rather than exactly right, and it can miss exact terms such as product codes, names or error numbers.

**Reranking** fixes the first. Retrieve generously (say the top 20), then let a stronger, slower model re-score those candidates and keep the best few:

```python
query_engine = index.as_query_engine(similarity_top_k=20,
    node_postprocessors=[SentenceTransformerRerank(model="cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2", top_n=4)])
```

A **cross-encoder** reads the question and a passage *together* and outputs a relevance score, which is more accurate than comparing two separate embeddings. Options: `SentenceTransformerRerank` (local model, needs `sentence-transformers`), `LLMRerank` (asks your LLM to rank), and hosted rerankers such as Cohere's via integration packages.

**Hybrid search** fixes the second. Combine vector search with **BM25**, a classic ranking method that rewards exact word matches. Then merge the two ranked lists:

- `BM25Retriever` (package `llama-index-retrievers-bm25`) does the keyword part.
- `QueryFusionRetriever([vector_retriever, bm25_retriever], mode="reciprocal_rerank")` merges them with **reciprocal rank fusion**: documents ranked high in either list rise to the top. Set `num_queries=1` to disable its default behaviour of generating extra query variations with the LLM.

Many vector databases (Qdrant, Weaviate, Elasticsearch, pgvector setups) offer hybrid search built in, which scales better than BM25 held in memory.

Measure before and after with a retrieval evaluation; both techniques add **latency** (waiting time per question).
concepts.code:
# pip install llama-index-retrievers-bm25 sentence-transformers
from llama_index.core import Document, VectorStoreIndex
from llama_index.core.node_parser import SentenceSplitter
from llama_index.core.postprocessor import SentenceTransformerRerank
from llama_index.core.query_engine import RetrieverQueryEngine
from llama_index.core.retrievers import QueryFusionRetriever
from llama_index.retrievers.bm25 import BM25Retriever

docs = [Document(text="Error E-4031 means the printer drum is worn."),
        Document(text="Replace toner when prints look faded."),
        Document(text="Paper jams: open tray 2 and remove the sheet.")]
nodes = SentenceSplitter(chunk_size=256).get_nodes_from_documents(docs)
index = VectorStoreIndex(nodes)

hybrid = QueryFusionRetriever(
    [index.as_retriever(similarity_top_k=10), BM25Retriever.from_defaults(nodes=nodes, similarity_top_k=10)],
    similarity_top_k=10, num_queries=1, mode="reciprocal_rerank", use_async=False)

rerank = SentenceTransformerRerank(model="cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2", top_n=2)
qe = RetrieverQueryEngine.from_args(hybrid, node_postprocessors=[rerank])
resp = qe.query("What does E-4031 mean?")
print(resp.source_nodes[0].node.text)   # Error E-4031 means the printer drum is worn.
takeaways: Rerank: retrieve many, re-score with a cross-encoder or LLM, keep few
Hybrid: BM25 keyword + vector results merged by reciprocal rank fusion
`QueryFusionRetriever(..., num_queries=1, mode="reciprocal_rerank")`
pitfalls: Adding a reranker but keeping similarity_top_k at 2, leaving the reranker nothing to choose from.

quiz.q: Users search for part numbers like 'X-220B' and vector search misses them. What helps most?
options: Hybrid search adding BM25 keyword matching
quiz.explain: Keyword ranking matches exact tokens like part numbers that embeddings may not capture.

concepts.name: Evaluating RAG
concepts.summary: Measure how often retrieval finds the right chunks, and judge answers with faithfulness and relevancy evaluators, over a set of test questions.
concepts.why: Without measurements, every chunking, model or prompt change is a guess that may make things worse.
concepts.body:
RAG has two parts to measure: did retrieval find the right chunks, and did the LLM answer well from them?

**Retrieval scores** need questions paired with the node ids that *should* be found:

- `hit_rate`: how often a correct node appears in the top k results.
- `mrr` (**MRR**, mean reciprocal rank): rewards finding it near the top; 1 if first, 0.5 if second, and so on.

```python
evaluator = RetrieverEvaluator.from_metric_names(["hit_rate", "mrr"], retriever=retriever)
result = await evaluator.aevaluate(query="...", expected_ids=[node_id])
```

These need no LLM, so they are cheap to run on hundreds of questions.

**Response evaluators** use an LLM as a judge:

- `FaithfulnessEvaluator` (**faithfulness**): is the answer supported by the retrieved context, or did the model make things up?
